neighbours.label: Evokes a concrete physical sense while explaining or extending a figurative expression.
fire: Describing a difficult colleague as prickly compares their manner to the sharp spines of a cactus.
When the teacher says an idea has roots, she does not mean that it grows underground.
Calling a politician slippery borrows the image of a surface too smooth to grip.
The expression carrying emotional baggage pictures old worries as heavy suitcases dragged along a journey.
A person with a heart of gold has kindness, rather than a chest containing precious metal.
To say the proposal has teeth is to imagine it biting, not to describe an actual mouth.
The phrase a weight off my shoulders treats relief as setting down a heavy load.
When a joke falls flat, nothing has literally dropped onto a level floor.
quiet: The cactus beside the window has sharp spines that make it difficult to handle safely.
During the lesson, the class dug carefully around the plant to see its roots underground.
Rain made the polished surface slippery, so the worker held tightly to the handrail.
Passengers carried heavy suitcases down the platform before loading their baggage onto the train.
The jeweler placed a small heart made of gold inside a padded presentation box.
A photograph in the biology textbook showed the teeth and mouth of an adult animal.
The porter set down a heavy load and rubbed his tired shoulders before continuing.
A dropped plate landed flat on the level floor and broke beside the kitchen door.

notes: The card mixes literal definitions, extended metaphors and physical reinterpretations of abstract language. Probes supported explicitly contrasting figurative and physical senses more strongly than literal description alone. This is a contextual hypothesis, not a claim about one vocabulary item.
